sceneHappening: Endure like a soldier, an athlete, and a farmer; hand on the teaching; avoid word-fights; be a vessel for honor
summary: "You therefore, my child, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus. The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also." Timothy must "endure hardship as a good soldier of Christ Jesus. No soldier on duty entangles himself in the affairs of life, that he may please him who enrolled him as a soldier." An athlete "isn't crowned unless he has competed by the rules," and "the farmer who labors must be the first to get a share of the crops." Timothy is to "remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, of the offspring of David, according to my Good News, in which I suffer hardship to the point of chains as a criminal. But God's word isn't chained." So Paul endures all things "for the chosen ones' sake." A trustworthy saying follows: "For if we died with him, we will also live with him. If we endure, we will also reign with him. If we deny him, he also will deny us. If we are faithless, he remains faithful; for he can't deny himself." Timothy is to remind them "that they don't argue about words, to no profit, to the subverting of those who hear," to "present yourself approved by God, a workman who doesn't need to be ashamed, properly handling the Word of Truth," and to "shun empty chatter." Hymenaeus and Philetus have "erred concerning the truth, saying that the resurrection is already past." Yet "God's firm foundation stands, having this seal, 'The Lord knows those who are his,' and, 'Let every one who names the name of the Lord depart from unrighteousness.'" In a large house there are vessels of gold and silver, wood and clay, and "if anyone therefore purges himself from these, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified, and suitable for the master's use." Timothy is to "flee from youthful lusts; but pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace," to "refuse foolish and ignorant questionings," and as the Lord's servant not to quarrel but "be gentle toward all, able to teach, patient, in gentleness correcting those who oppose him: perhaps God may give them repentance leading to a full knowledge of the truth, and they may recover themselves out of the devil's snare."
whySettingMatters: Paul gives Timothy three pictures of ordinary workers: the soldier who is single-minded, the athlete who obeys the rules, and the farmer who works first and eats after. Each is about staying with a task for the long haul, not about glory. The line about teaching "faithful men... who will be able to teach others also" names four generations in one sentence (Paul, Timothy, faithful people, others), the shape of how the faith was meant to be passed on. The "trustworthy saying" in 2:11-13 is probably an early hymn or confession; it ends with a comfort that echoes the promise in 1:12: even when we are faithless, he remains faithful. Verse 12's "if we deny him, he also will deny us" echoes Jesus' own words in Matthew 10:33. The claim by Hymenaeus and Philetus that "the resurrection is already past" has been read as a teaching that the resurrection was only spiritual, something already experienced in baptism or in new life (compare Colossians 2:12 and Ephesians 2:6, which they may have misused). "The large house" with vessels of different uses (2:20-21) has been read as the church, with some members dishonorable, or as the world; the instruction to "purge" oneself is about moving away from false teaching and wrongdoing. "Properly handling the Word of Truth" translates a Greek word, orthotomeo, that means to "cut straight," as a road builder or stonemason would; the picture is exact and careful work. In 2:25-26 the aim of correction is not defeat but repentance, which matters for how disagreements in the church are handled.

questions: Soldier, athlete, farmer: which picture speaks most to the kind of endurance you need right now?
Paul pictures the faith passed through four "generations." Who handed it to you, and who might you pass it to?
"If we are faithless, he remains faithful." What does that promise settle, and what does it not settle?
Paul's advice for opponents is gentleness, with the hope of repentance. How does that change how you would handle a disagreement in your church?
